case.case_title: Senerath v. Chandraratne, Commissioner of Excise and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, Senerath v. Chandraratne, Commissioner of Excise and Others, 1995

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was subjected to unlawful discrimination violating Article 12(1) by the refusal to renew his liquor licences allegedly at the instigation of the President's political influence.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that the refusal to renew his liquor licences was discriminatory and violated his right to equality before the law under Article 12(1), as licences were issued only to persons recommended by the ruling party's members, and that he was singled out due to political displeasure.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the President has personal immunity under Article 35 of the Constitution, barring proceedings against her, and that the petitioner sought relief only against officials, not the President. They also contended that the burden of proof was on the petitioner and that there was no obligation for the President to respond to allegations.
key_facts: Petitioner’s liquor licence renewal was refused allegedly due to political reasons linked to the President.
Leave to proceed was granted by the Supreme Court on 21 July 1995 for alleged infringements of Articles 12(1) and 12(2).
The Attorney-General objected to the continuation of proceedings citing presidential immunity under Article 35.
The petitioner sought relief against officials, not the President directly.
The Court considered the scope of Article 35 immunity and the burden of proof on the petitioner.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court interpreted Article 12(1) as guaranteeing equality before the law and equal protection, but emphasized that the petitioner must prove discrimination. The Court held that the President’s immunity under Article 35 does not bar proceedings against officials, and that the petitioner’s claim was against officials, not the President personally.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the petitioner had not filed proceedings against the President but against officials, and that the burden to prove discriminatory conduct was on the petitioner. Mere suspicion was insufficient. The Court rejected the argument that the President must respond to allegations or that the immunity was being evaded.
principles_established: Article 12(1) protects against unlawful discrimination and guarantees equality before the law.
The burden of proving discrimination lies heavily on the petitioner.
Presidential immunity under Article 35 is personal and does not extend to officials.
The Court cannot entertain indirect attempts to circumvent constitutional immunities.
precedents_cited: Hettiarachchi v. Seneviratne S.C. Application No. 127/94
Ashutosh v. State of Delhi AIR 1953 SC 451

outcome.holding: The Court overruled the preliminary objection and allowed the petitioner to proceed with the fundamental rights application under Article 12(1), holding that the claim against officials for alleged discriminatory refusal to renew licences was maintainable.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Preliminary objection overruled; petition set down for hearing on the merits.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) is central to the petitioner’s claim of unlawful discrimination in the refusal to renew liquor licences, and the Court’s reasoning focused on whether the petitioner was denied equal protection of the law.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner alleged that refusal to renew his licences was discriminatory and violative of Article 12(1). The Court held that the petitioner must prove such discrimination and that the claim against officials was maintainable despite the President’s immunity under Article 35.
